sections.h2: Which county is your Tulsa house in?
sections.html:
Tulsa is Oklahoma's second-largest city, with 413,066 residents in the 2020 census and a metro area of 1,034,123. The city covers 201.85 square miles and reaches into four counties: Tulsa, Osage, Rogers and Wagoner.

Your county picks the office that values the house and the office that mails the tax bill. Nearly all Tulsa houses are in Tulsa County, yet a parcel near the city limits may fall under Osage, Rogers or Wagoner County instead, and each has its own assessor and treasurer. Read the county name on your tax statement before you phone any office.

School boundaries are split the same way. Tulsa, Berryhill, Bixby, Broken Arrow, Jenks, Owasso and Union districts serve the Tulsa County part of the city, and Tulsa Public Schools serves the Osage County part. Buyers often ask which district an address belongs to, so know the answer before you list.

Tulsa is a set of very different areas, and where a house sits changes how it is priced and who shops for it.

  • Downtown: about 1.4 square miles inside the Inner Dispersal Loop, with the Oil Capital Historic District, Blue Dome, Tulsa Arts District and Greenwood. Nearby are Owen Park, The Pearl, The Heights and Kendall-Whittier.
  • Midtown: the historic residential core, with early 20th-century homes in styles from art deco to Greek Revival in Maple Ridge, Swan Lake, Cherry Street, Brookside and Lortondale.
  • South Tulsa: mostly built since the 1970s, with lower-density suburban housing and retail.
  • East of Highway 169: a diverse area with much of the city's manufacturing.
  • West Tulsa: west of the Arkansas River, with large parks, reserves and oil refineries.

A century-old Midtown house and a 1980s south Tulsa ranch get different inspection questions. The older house draws questions about wiring, plumbing and foundations. The newer one draws questions about roof age and heating and cooling.

Tulsa has a humid subtropical climate, and spring and early summer bring severe thunderstorms with large hail, damaging winds and sometimes tornadoes. May is the wettest month at 5.9 inches. Hail damage to a roof is one of the most common things a Tulsa seller has to deal with.

Flooding shaped the city's rules. A stalled front dropped 15 inches of rain overnight in 1984, killing 14 people and destroying 7,000 buildings. Tulsa then built one of the nation's most extensive flood control systems, and FEMA honored it for floodplain management in the early 1990s and again in 2000.

If your house sits near a creek or in a mapped flood area, expect the buyer's lender to ask about flood insurance. Triple-digit heat averages 11 days a year, so the air conditioning also lands on the inspection list. Pull any storm photos, repair estimates and insurance claim records before you list, because buyers ask for them.

sections.h2: Tulsa code enforcement and open violations
sections.html:
Tulsa's Code Enforcement handles nuisance, zoning and property maintenance rules for occupied, commercial and vacant properties. It investigates about 22,000 violations across more than 18,000 cases a year. Reports go to 311 or tulsa311.com.

Violation stepWhat happens
Priority 1Unsecured structures, vehicles on blocks, blocked sidewalks, raw sewage
Priority 3Tall grass, trash, junk and debris, handled in order received
NoticeOwner gets 10 days to comply
ExtensionsUp to two 10-day extensions at $64 each, not available for every violation
AbatementIf the city does the work, the owner pays the cost plus a $300 processing fee

The city's "Up to Code" brochure adds that grass over 12 inches, unsecured vacant structures and inoperable vehicles stored outdoors are violations. An owner must board up a vacant structure after a fire, and openings left by a break-in must be secured right away.

Anyone can search a property's code cases back to 2018 through the city's self-service portal. Buyers can do it too, so assume they will see an open case on your address. Clearing it before you list avoids a surprise late in the deal.

sections.h2: Tulsa County property tax and key dates
sections.html:
In Tulsa County, the Assessor sets the value as of January 1 and the Treasurer collects the bill. The Assessor's calendar runs like this:

  • January 1 to March 15: apply for most exemptions, including homestead. Late applications generally wait until the next year.
  • First Monday in April: last day for an informal appeal if you were not mailed an increase notice.
  • May 31: the Board of Equalization adjourns unless it extends to June 30.
  • September 15 to October 1: owner and address updates pause while the tax roll is prepared.
  • October and November: the roll goes to the Treasurer, who mails bills.

At least half the tax must be paid before January 1, and if you pay in halves, the second half must be paid before April 1. Because ownership changes pause each fall, a seller who closes in that window should confirm the bill still goes to the right person. The title company normally prorates the tax between buyer and seller.

sections.h2: Ways to sell a house in Tulsa
sections.html:
The three main routes are an agent listing, a sale by owner and a cash offer. With so many different neighborhoods, local pricing matters more than a citywide average.

  • Agent listing: reaches the most buyers, with prep, showings and a financed buyer's appraisal to get through.
  • By owner: avoids a commission but puts pricing and paperwork on you.
  • Cash offer: built for houses with repairs, open code cases, tenants, hail damage or an estate to settle.

A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal, the back-and-forth over repairs and the weeks waiting on loan approval. The title company handles payoffs at closing, so a lien or an unpaid city charge comes out of your proceeds instead of stopping the deal.

sections.h2: Closing day and what a cash sale skips
sections.html:
Closing happens at a title company. You sign the deed, the title company pays off any mortgage or lien, and the rest of the proceeds come to you. Tax for the year is split between you and the buyer there, so bring your latest county tax statement. If an open code case is still on the property, ask the title company how it will be handled at the table.

A buyer paying cash does not need a lender's sign-off, so there is no appraisal that can come in low and no loan that can fall through. That is the main reason owners with hail-damaged roofs, tenants in place or an estate to settle choose it.

sections.h2: Documents to gather before you decide
sections.html:
Gather three papers before you talk to any buyer: the code case history for your address, the county tax statement, and whatever storm or insurance claim records you have. Offers for Tulsa houses tend to move on those three.

Open the city's code portal and print each open case. Next, check the county on the tax statement and confirm whether the bill is current. Last, collect hail photos, roof estimates and claim letters. With those in hand, you can compare an agent listing, a sale by owner and a cash offer on real numbers rather than guesses.

faqs.q: Is Tulsa only in Tulsa County?
faqs.a: No. The city reaches into Tulsa, Osage, Rogers and Wagoner Counties. Your tax statement shows which county's assessor and treasurer serve your address.

faqs.q: How do I report or look up a code violation in Tulsa?
faqs.a: Call 311 or use tulsa311.com to report one. The city's self-service portal lets you search code cases by address, with results going back to 2018.

faqs.q: How long do I have to fix a Tulsa code violation?
faqs.a: The notice gives the owner 10 days to comply. You can buy up to two 10-day extensions at $64 each, though some violations, such as unsecured structures, are not eligible.

faqs.q: When must I file for the homestead exemption in Tulsa County?
faqs.a: The Tulsa County Assessor accepts applications all year, but to count for the current year the application must be filed by March 15 or within 30 days of a valuation-increase notice.

faqs.q: Does hail damage stop me from selling a Tulsa house?
faqs.a: No. You can repair the roof and list the house, or sell it as is to a buyer who accounts for the damage. Keep photos, estimates and any insurance paperwork handy.
